newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: GM says Renault closure signals shakeout start.
newsitem.headline: GM says Renault closure signals shakeout start.

text.p: General Motors the world's biggest car producer, said on Tuesday that job losses at Renault and Ford F N signal the start of the long-awaited shakeout in Europe, but said it hopes that it is healthy enough to avoid similar action.
Europe's car makers find themselves in a vicious circle of their own making, producing more cars than they can sell at a profit.
To keep plants running at close to capacity, car companies have engaged in a ruinous slashing of prices and expensive incentives.
"Some say there is excess capacity in Europe of three to four million units," General Motors Europe president Richard Donnelly told a press conference.

"We are seeing in the announced plant closings (at Ford and Renault) and price cuts the start of some kind of shakeout (in Europe)," Donnelly said in reply to a question at the press conference, held on the eve of the annual Geneva car show.
"It is not our goal to close plants. If we have to we might, but this is not on the immediate horizon," Donnelly said.
News last week that French mass car manufacturer Renault would close a factory at Vilvoorde, Belgium with the loss of 3,100 jobs, ignited a political storm.

The Belgian government threatened to sue Renault, in which the French government has a 46 percent stake, alleging that the company had violated Belgian and European Union legislation requiring companies to consult worker representatives about closures and layoffs.
Belgium also said it would seek new European laws to stop multinational corporations from shifting plants and jobs across national borders.
In January, Ford said it would slash 980 jobs at its Halewood, England plant.
Politicians across Europe should start rehearsing speeches with plenty of spontaneous anger, because industry experts say more job losses are imminent, and the health of the industry depends on them.
Car sales in western Europe peaked at 13.5 million in 1992, but plummeted almost two million or 15 percent the following year, the biggest drop in sales for 50 years.
Since then sales have struggled to regain the record pace, and in 1996 had crept back up to around 12.8 million. Most experts expect sales to just top 13 million in 1997.
But to spur sales, car companies slashed prices and offered tempting incentives. Governments were persuaded to offer rebates to buyers to swap ten year old bangers for new, cleaner small cars.
This skewed sales towards smaller, less profitable models, and effectively stole sales from the future.
Experts say unless drastic action is taken soon to cut overcapacity, bankruptcies cannot be ruled out.

This cull of production could take the form of the long promised shakeout of consolidations and mergers, with the weaker of the big six mass car makers finally losing their independence and succumbing to takeover. This would deliver an industry where the major players had market shares approaching 20 percent, but it couldn't avoid the pain of closures.

In 1996 Germany's Volkswagen was market leader in western Europe with 17.2 percent, followed by General Motors Europe's Opel and Vauxhall brands with 12.5 percent, France's Peugeot Citroen (11.9 percent), Ford (11.6), and Fiat SpA of Italy (11.2). Renault of France brought up the rear with 10.1 percent.
Professor Krish Bhaskar from the Motor Industry Research Unit in Nice, France, said luxury car makers don't share in this overcapacity bind, but predicts plant closures for others.

"The specialists like Bayerische Motoren-Werke AG (BMW) BMWG.F, (VW's) Audi, Mercedes DAIG.F don't have any spare capacity, but for the rest, Fiat will have to close one or two, and Peugeot as well," Bhaskar said.
GM's Donnelly told the press conference he didn't expect Opel or Vauxhall factories to be closing doors any time soon.

"We've got pretty good if not the best capacity utilisation in Europe. We want to keep all our plants fully utilised. At the moment there is a pretty good balance between production and demand," Donnelly said.
